{{Short description|American physicist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date = March 2019}}

'''Evan O'Neill Kane''' (December 23, 1924 – March 23, 2006), known as '''E. O. Kane''' in his publications, was an American physicist who established some of the basic understanding of the theory of [[semiconductor]]s that are now used in consumer and other electronics. He was one of the main developers of the [[k·p perturbation theory|'''k·p''' perturbation theory]] which is used to calculate band structures.<ref>{{Citation |last=Kane |first=E. O. |title=Chapter 3 The k •p Method |date=1966-01-01 |volume=1 |pages=75–100 |editor-last=Willardson |editor-first=R. K. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0080878408623765 |access-date=2024-08-15 |series=Semiconductors and Semimetals |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/S0080-8784(08)62376-5 |bibcode=1966SemS....1...75K |isbn=978-0-12-752101-5 |editor2-last=Beer |editor2-first=Albert C.|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Ancestry ==
Kane's great, great uncle, [[Elisha Kent Kane]], was an arctic explorer, writing books in the 1850s about his journeys. His great grandfather, [[Thomas Leiper Kane]], who founded the town of [[Kane, Pennsylvania]], was an [[American Civil War]] General.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kane, Pennsylvania |url=https://visitanf.com/kane/ |access-date=2024-08-15 |website=Allegheny National Forest Visitors Bureau |language=en-US}}</ref> He also helped with the [[Underground Railroad]] and successfully urged the [[Presidency of James Buchanan|Buchanan Administration]] not to go to war with the [[Mormons]] in [[Salt Lake City]]. Kane's grandfather, also named [[Evan O'Neill Kane]], was a doctor who was so enamoured of the idea of [[local anesthesia]] that he surgically removed his own [[Appendix (anatomy)|appendix]] to show its effectiveness.

== Life ==
Kane was born on December 23, 1924<ref name="scitation.org">{{cite web|url=http://physicstoday.scitation.org/department/people-and-history?Ppub=%5B20060101%20TO%2020061231%5D&sortBy=&pageSize=100|title=Physics Today Daily Edition Departments}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Obituary of Evan O' Neill Kane|doi=10.1063/pt.4.2301|year=2013|journal=Physics Today |volume=2006 |issue=3 |article-number=18014 }}</ref><ref name="bradleyfuneralhomes.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.bradleyfuneralhomes.com/descendant/299580/Evan/|title=Bradley & Son Funeral Homes}}</ref> in [[Kane, Pennsylvania]]. His father, Thomas Leiper Kane, died in 1933 of [[pneumonia]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bowen |first1=Norman R. |last2=Zobell |first2=Albert L. |last3=Jr. |title=General Thomas L. Kane: the Pioneer |url=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/ensign/1971/10/general-thomas-l-kane-the-pioneer?lang=eng |access-date=2024-08-15 |website=www.churchofjesuschrist.org |language=en}}</ref> He later moved with his mother and siblings to [[Daytona Beach, Florida]], where he stayed through high school.

=== Career ===
Kane was an undergraduate at [[Princeton University]], and interrupted his education to serve in the army during [[World War II]]. He graduated from [[Princeton University]] in 1948, and went directly to [[Cornell University]] to study towards his PhD in physics, which was awarded in 1953 on an experimental project related to [[vacuum tube]] technology. Kane then joined the [[General Electric Research Laboratory]] in Schenectady, New York. There he began contributing to the theoretical underpinnings of the then-new field of [[semiconductor]] research. He published widely in scientific journals. Perhaps his best known paper was published in 1956 on a technique to calculate the structure of solids.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kane|first1=E. O.|year=1956|title=Energy band structure in p-type germanium and silicon|journal=Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids|volume=1|issue=1–2|pages=82–99|bibcode=1956JPCS....1...82K|doi=10.1016/0022-3697(56)90014-2}}</ref> This technique is referred to as the [[K·p perturbation theory|'''k·p''' method]] for band structure calculations. 

Kane left General Electric in 1959 to join [[Hughes Aircraft Company|Hughes Aircraft]] in California and then moved to the Theoretical Physics Department in [[Bell Labs#Formal organization and location changes|Bell Laboratories]] in Murray Hill, New Jersey in 1961. He continued his semiconductor research at Bell Labs, at the interface between experimental and theoretical physics, until [[AT&T]] was broken up. He then worked for [[Bellcore|BellCore]] until he retired in 1984.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

=== Personal life ===
Kane married Anne Bassler in 1950 in [[Lancaster, Pennsylvania]]. They lived together for over 40 years in [[New Providence, New Jersey]], where they raised three children and coauthored one paper.<ref>EO Kane and AB Kane, "Direct calculation of Wannier Functions; Si valence bands, Physical Review B, 17, 2691 (1978).</ref> 

In 1974, he became ranked second in the country in the 50 and over marathon category. He spent most of the rest of his life working in childcare for infants, toddlers and young children including his grandchildren and church group. He died in 2006 at the age of 81. The cause of death was complications secondary to [[Myeloproliferative neoplasm|myeloproliferative disease]] and [[Myelodysplastic syndrome|myelodysplasia]].<ref name="scitation.org" /><ref name="bradleyfuneralhomes.com" /> He had three children. <ref name="bradleyfuneralhomes.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.bradleyfuneralhomes.com/descendant/299580/Evan/|title=Bradley & Son Funeral Homes}}</ref>

== Kane model ==
Kane used the '''k·p''' perturbation method to determine what became known as the '''Kane model''' or '''Kane Hamiltonian''' of the structure of energy bands of semiconductors.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kane|first1=E. O.|year=1957|title=Band structure of indium antimonide|journal=Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids|volume=1|issue=4|pages=249–261|bibcode=1957JPCS....1..249K|doi=10.1016/0022-3697(57)90013-6}}</ref> The Kane Hamiltonian describes the [[valence and conduction bands]] in sp<sup>3</sup> bonded semiconductors: the [[Group (periodic table)|group]] IV, III-V and II-VI semiconductors. This 1957 publication is still prominent in scientific literature and textbooks more than 50 years after its discovery (the paper has about 3377 citations<ref name="google" /> despite the fact that modern [[citation index]]es undercount citations for papers published before the mid-1990s). The model is now often cited via books where it is discussed, most notably in Yu's and [[Manuel Cardona|Cardona]]'s book, ''Fundamentals of Semiconductors''.<ref>Peter Y. Yu and Manuel Cardona, "Fundamentals of Semiconductors, Physics and Materials Properties, Springer, {{ISBN|978-3-642-00709-5}} (Print)  978-3-642-00710-1 (Online)</ref>

In their book on the '''k·p''' method, Voon and Willatzen<ref>Lok C. Lew Yan Voon and Morten Willatzen, "The k.p Method" Electronic Properties of Semiconductors, Springer, Springer-Verlag Berlin, Heidelberg, 2009. {{doi|10.1007/978-3-540-92872-0}}</ref> devote several chapters to explaining Kane models. They note that Kane's quasi-degenerate [[Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbation theory]] approach worked well for semiconductors with small [[band gap]]s. Kane improved previous valence band models by adding the lowest conduction band. This model was extended later to take into account the non-parabolicity of materials such as [[gallium arsenide]] (GaAs). The model explains essentially most of the materials used in semiconductor technology. The theoretical literature describing the electronics and optical responses of these semiconductors all rely heavily on this model, as does the very active field of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum]] phenomena in size-limited crystalline structures.
